text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London reversed an earlier downward trend and closed sharply higher after speculative short- covering in New York pushed prices up. March added $20 to close at $1,454 per tonne, while May closed $23 higher at 1,556 per tonne. Trading was fairly quiet with the day's volume at a modest 5,099 lots. Traders said technically the market's outlook remains constructive with resistance pegged at the recent high of $1,630 a tonne basis March while support is seen at $1,424 per tonne.

Arabica futures in New York closed sharply higher on reports of grower unrest in Colombia. March added 6.25 cents/lb to close at 150.80 cents/lb, while May added 5.60 cents/lb to close at 144.80 cents/lb. Grower dissatisfaction in Colombia is nothing new although non- performing on debt makes the situation a bit more complicated. However, it is not yet clear whether this will have any impact on the crop. Many traders expect prices to continue to rise with the upside target seen at between 175 and 200 cents/lb.

BRAZIL - The first estimate for the 1997/98 (May/April) Brazilian coffee crop will be released on February 19 by the Brazilian Association of Coffee Exporters (Abecafe). For the first time, the association counted on the aid of various companies, who visited farms throughout Brazil.

COLOMBIA - Colombia's leading Independent Coffee Growers Association declared a moratorium on debt payments as part of a campaign of 'civil disobedience' aimed at helping cash- strapped farmers. The decision, which would affect about $200 million in past-due loans owned to the state-run Caja Agraria bank and Banco Cafetero was adopted at a meeting of the independent Unidad Cafetera Nacional. It is feared that grower dissatisfaction could have an impact on 1996/97 production estimated by the Coffee Federation at 12.5 million bags. However, trade sources said the total could be no more than 10 million bags. This was ascribed partly to unusual heavy rains during the flowering period, the debtors' strike and the abandonment of a growing number of farms by impoverished growers fed up with the insecurity of the countryside as well as difficulties to get credit to fight broca that has affected more than half of Colombia's coffee plantations.

UNITED STATES - The United States imported 1.590 million bags of coffee in November 1996, 0.7 percent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 17.459 million bags, 13 percent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 6 percent to 15.421 million bags. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/November 1996 were Guatemala (1.487 vs 1.437 million bags), Mexico (3.414 vs 2.533 million bags), Brazil (1.600 vs 2.208 million bags), Colombia (2.623 vs 2.224 million bags) and Indonesia (1.137 vs 0.418 million bags). The country exported 1.889 million bags of coffee in January/November 1996, 18 percent more than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 fell sharply by 22 percent to 1.841 million bags.
